First of all, I'm not going to talk about how the game it was or what are the differences between now and then, just going to talk about the current state of the game.

I'm going to divide my comment in 5 different topics: Main story, exploration, combat, multiplayer and ship and tools.

Story: In my humble opinion, the story of this game is interesting, engaging and at the end you will feel like when you have finished a book in which you were totally immersed and you will start to think and typical philosophical questions will come to your mind.
The time you'll time to finish the main story will depend on you and how fast you can progress, for me it took around 30 hours but it can be done much faster. Besides, the main story will help you discover and how to do many things in the game so it is helpful to get you started with the universe of no man's sky. 

Exploration: A lot can be said about the exploration as it is supposed to be the main attraction of this game. In my opinion the exploration is fun at first and you will discover different planets, empty ones, moons, toxic, hazardous, paradises etc... You will also find different flora and fauna different between planets and of course different kind of resources. Notice that the underwater environment are usually awesome (at least I love them) and there is also submarine fauna and flora. 

However, there is something I really think it's not well implemented in this game and it has so much potential that I hate it. 
The problem is that after you have seen a type of planet, most of the planet of that kind will be incredibly similar (sometimes you won't even be able to distinguish them without looking at the name of the planet). The faun and flora yes is different but.... there are some flora that is shared between all the planets (even from different galaxies) and even in 'empty' planets you can find this flora underground, which in my opinion is absurd to call them 'empty' or 'desolated' or 'dead' like it's called in-game. 

There is also the thing that there is only one biome per planet so it doesn't matter where you land your ship, you'll find the same stuff. Some people might say that usually in other planets in real life there is only one biome and that the earth is different, but I have to disagree with that statement. Biome is related to plans and animal and how these interfere and relate with the environment, so if we find in real life a planet with animal and plants there will be for sure different biomes. 

The terrain is also usually a bit dull, as there are not  actual mountains or ravines or waterfalls.... so do not expect to find much of this. 

Exploration of space  itself is interesting but there is no much to find out there to be honest. No gas planets a far as I know, and no double star system or systems with more than 6 planets. In my opinion gas planets should be there even if we can't do anything with them, it would give the game realism. 

In general, exploration is fun and you will find interesting things but there so much this game lacks about exploration, that is quite a big missed opportunity in my opinion. 

Combat: No much to say about this, you can be a pirate and fight freighters and other pirates in pace, sack depots in planets and fight the sentinels, but it's not really that complex or deep. It's not supposed to be the main focus of the game so fair enough. 

Multiplayer: currently the multiplayer is fully implemented and there is crossplay between consoles and PC. You can go with friends to their freighters or their bases, do missions of the Anomaly, explore together or do whatever you want with them. No PVP as far as I know, is a cooperative game. You can also trade with people (exchanging resources or tools).

Ships and tools: There are many ships you can have and upgrades that can be done, even a living ship and upgrades for the living ship. You can also have a capital freighter with a float under you command that will go on missions to get you new stuff and money. 

You also have a multi-tool to extract mineral and use it as a gun. There are upgrades for this tool and different types.
There is one thing about some resources and items, and the problem is that some of them are only useful to sell them, to earn more money. I think they should have some kind of use in the game.

The base building system is actually really good and you can make absolutely impressive buildings (take a look at youtube) and you can share with the rest of the community as everyone shares the same universe (you just need to upload your base in game).



To sum up, this game is worth playing it even if you only want to play the main story. there are plenty of game in which you will spend a lot less time playing their story than in this game and ~30 hours is a good amount for the story of a game. After that you are left with a universe of 255 galaxies filled with systems and planets and races (3 intelligent ones apart from the player) and I think it's worth for everyone that likes the space, a bit of exploration or just for fun. 

Still, I think the universe could be a lot better and the variety should be higher for such a big universe.

I'm gonna start my review with the list of all the negative aspects I've encountered so far in my playthrough, and then will try to explain why I still really loved this game. A tl;dr version is: "remember that part in Mass Effect when you had to ride in a Mako on some random planets, harvesting resources and doing generic quests? Well if you liked it, this is the game for you".

[list]
[*]The game is still pretty buggy. I've no idea what it was like on release, but my guess is that over the years it went from "totally unplayable" to "slightly annoying sometimes". I've yet to encounter any serious issues. The ones I've seen were either graphics glitching or weird pathfinding (like creatures dropping through the ceiling to the cave you're exploring). One annoying thing that I've encountered a couple of times was a randomly generated building clipping through the environment (in particular, a trading outpost spawned inside a mountain and I had to dig it up with terrain manipulator in order to get to the quest NPC). It's a little immersion-breaking but thank God it's not very common and mostly doesn't hinder you in any way.
[*]The console-style interface is a mess, especially when building stuff. It's clunky and tedious to use. I know it's a crossplay title, but come on. Having to go through a million tiny scrolling menus in order to get to a part that you want to build is a huge pain, there's no excuse for that.
[*]Almost everything in this game requires quite a bit of grinding on giant procedurally generated planets. Grind is the only real challenge in this game, and since it's a sandbox, you mostly have to set your own goals. There is a plot and some general storyline quests, but no space opera stuff for sure.
[*]As with all games that use procedural generation, things can and will get repetitive. The universe is almost infinite, but the amount of things you can do there isn't. 
[*]Multiplayer is very laggy as of July 2020. I haven't tried playing with friends, but joining random parties wasn't pleasant. 
[*]First 15 minutes of the game legit made me wanna refund it. This is I think one of the worst starting 15 minutes in any game I've ever played. You've got to overcome it in order to enjoy the rest.
[/list]
So, in spite of all these problems, why do I still recommend No Man's Sky? Because it's quite simply a unique experience. This is one of the most relaxing, immersive games I know. It feels great to explore new systems and planets, building bases, finding loot and doing simple quests. The mere excitement you get from jumping across the galaxy into the unknown is worth it. Also the game looks gorgeous and sometimes makes you just stop to enjoy the scenery, especially with some graphical mods.

All I said about grinding and generic nature of the game turns from a downside into a feature if you enjoy that kind of stuff.  I once spent a whole evening riding on my rover trying to find the last species on the planet for my collection. During this expedition I stumbled upon a couple ruins and outposts, farmed some resources and got in a few storms. If this sounds like an evening well-spent to you, then you'd enjoy No Man's Sky as well. 

In conclusion, I'd say buy this game during sale if you like slow exploration and don't mind procedural generation and a few bugs here and there.

Honestly, it is awesome how much effort was put into this game by the devs, especially considering its TERRIBLE start. They are still actively creating content, and it is just awesome. Now that the game has been polished, I can definitely say it is much closer to what they advertised it would be when they first launched... plus a little extra.
The multiplayer can be buggy at times, but it is still super fun. 
I have poured hours into this game, and it is still finding little ways to surprise me. Whether it's a little hoppy mushroom creature sauntering past me as I collect oxygen for my biosuit, or it's raiders trying to ruin my day while I'm minding my business in space, No Man's Sky is always keeping me on my toes.
With the Nexus update, they added a lot of multiplayer functionality that people felt they were missing. It helps to mitigate the sometimes present feeling of loneliness that can come from playing this game for long periods of time.

Finally,
Let's talk about VR....
Short version: you need to have a stomach of steel.
The controls are moderately difficult to learn, especially if you are already used to playing the game conventionally.
Not only that, but I can only play for about ten minutes before I have severe motion sickness. I am the kind of person that struggles with motion sickness anyways, but this game is the worst that I have experienced so far. That being said, this game is also one of the most incredible that I've ever played in VR. If nothing else, this is simply because of the level of immersion it can provide. Nothing can compare to the feeling I had when I stood beside my starship and realized just how BIG it was. It felt like I was actually standing beside it. Maybe take some motion sickness meds and have a crack at it.

TLDR; What a good game. If this is on sale and you're on the fence, GO FOR IT.

I've been here since launch and let me tell you, this game has taken massive strides in the right direction. I think this game has set a great example that has inspired other developers that, despite a broken launch with several broken promises, they stick with it and make true to their vision and beyond, no matter how long it takes.

I don't think that this practice of releasing a broken game and fixing it over time is one to get in the habit of, but knowing NMS's story, I feel this is an exception with such a small team trying to fulfill a large vision. 

They continue to support the game with massive updates every few months that push it to go even beyond the promises they initially made. On top of that, with the game now available via crossplay, and easy access for many on platforms like Xbox's Gamepass, its highly accessible for the player to join with any of their friends, regardless of their platform of preference.

Now is it perfect? No. There's still features that were promised that aren't there quite yet, but with a couple friends, this game is a great time that is fun to explore and discover in. As the game continues to evolve, I'll gladly return to see what's new.

I feel like NMS's best qualities come from the sense of exploration, discovery, and building. Flying around, seeing new planets, and building up your base on the planet you discovered is a fun endeavor.

I feel like the weakest aspect though is the game play loop. It consists of the same cycle of landing somewhere to gather resources to go further into space in a long-term goal to reach the center of the galaxy. But I feel like having that objective in mind is the worst way to experience the game. Instead, push forward, but do so while doing coop missions, or by finding a nice planet to fully construct a base on. If your only goal is to reach the center, it will be a boring chore. Treat it like Minecraft but leave the "end goal" in the back of your mind.

It's pretty entertaining. It kept me exploring and learning new stuff for about 60+ hours. After that the game got kind of boring, but it still has it's worth and you can have a pretty nice time after that if you want to just keep exploring and stick some music on in the background. Very relaxing.

I hope that the game gets more variety in planets in the future. Not just variety in planets but variety on planets since I feel like there is no incentive to explore a planet, which is a shame considering we have some awesome vehicles to travel with.

It's hard to come by players, it's a very rare occurrence. But there's some great communities out there that have made settlements. Took me several hours of travelling in game and several weeks in real life to be able to get there which was kind of a cool experience, the journey itself was a cool experience and something worth writing about. Thinking back on it I should've wrote a log book detailing my journey and took pictures of the various planets I discovered, that would've been pretty nice.

On the topic of pictures, this game is a screenshot paradise. And on the internet there's plenty of communities that love reading and sharing that kind of stuff on forums.

I've also switched PVP on and have had a nail biting encounters with other players in these player communities which was pretty fun. Although it's rather basic, I quite like the starship combat it would be something I'd like to see expanded a bit more personally but since the game isn't really based off of that and it isn't common to see people willing to PVP I don't think it will be developed in depth. 

One negative aspect of this game is that the main questline is very long and very boring. The tutorial is good and gets you on your way to learn basic things, but after that it's just a case of 'go there, talk to that character, build that' and repeat until the end. Also I kept at the main questline to get the portal glyphs thinking they would be super convenient to have, however I learned that portals are practically useless because even if you use the portal to go somewhere, you can't do anything when you get there. So you'll have to travel there manually in order to do anything anyway. So the main questline is entirely pointless unless you want to complete the game.

All in all, it's turned out to be a real fun game. I put off buying it because I thought it would be boring, but I was pleasantly surprised. It's worth the money you pay for it.

I'd get this game if you're the adventurous type or if you have lots of time to kill and want something to keep your attention since this can be relaxing. Also survival players might find this fun, although it is a bit easy to survive even if you have perma-death on.
I wouldn't get this game if you're the type of person that wants constant action. You won't get that here I'm afraid.

Reviews.130080:
This game has quite a few features that make it such a good game compared to when I first saw it around.

PROS:
-Lots to do. This game really has anything you want in it. There is a story if you enjoy that, its also a crafting/survival game if you like that, you can explore and trade and play it like an RPG, you can do missions, play with friends, control fleets, and basically do whatever you want.
-Beautiful game. This game despite (or maybe because of) the indie like graphics looks amazing, I honestly enjoy just flying or driving around just to enjoy the view of my paradise planet, or even other planets. 
-Muliplayer, or not. You can play with friends across different platforms even, and they can help you with missions, base building, exploring, anything. This is a very fun MMO that I hope works very well with the cross play elements. 
-Easy grind. This game is not very intense with the grind needed for upgrades or building or anything. You can make a lot of headway while just playing for a few hours.
-Easy to play. A lot of games are confusing or very involved and need you to almost have inhuman prioritization and management skills with countless controls to remember. This is not one of those games, it is easy to keep track of everything and do anything you want without feeling overwhelmed.

CONS:
-Glitches do exist that are frustrating. Like getting caught on invisible lips and you cannot move, sometimes landing is a pain and takes multiple tries, and the depot missions are sometimes don't work since you cannot destroy the depot at all.
-Hefty game. I play this game on an Alienware Aurora R6 with a brand new graphics card and I will occasionally crash and lose saves, but it does not happen very often. 
-Saving is weird. You need to find save points or construct one in order to save your game, its not just a save and exit type of game, which can be annoying if you crash or just want to leave the game.
-Missions are repetitive, but replayable. The missions cycles between only a couple types, which can get boring, but they are very profitable and the missions are quite fun. Some diversity would be nice though. 

Conclusion:
This is quite a fun game for me so far and I will keep coming back to it for quite a while. It might have some flaws, but total respect to the developers for making this a game that I could no longer ignore and redeemed itself. If you want an all rounder game with the freedom to do what you want that is also in space, this is the game for you. 

Recommendation: Get this game on sale, $60 is not worth it when you can just wait a little bit until summer or the holidays (or the million other times Steam has a sale) and get it for $30.

It's great how much they worked on the game since its horrible launch. I'm sure it improved a lot and became way more complex. But I still found it to be extremely repetitive to the point that it's just not enjoyable to play after a couple of hours.

Supposedly there are endless variations of procedurally generated planets, yet the first planet I landed on in my second planetary system looked and felt basically indistinguishable from my initial planet. I did a quick google search and it turned out there are like a dozen different planet biomes, and every planet of a given biome looks pretty similar. Wow, great. There goes the selling point of discovering varied environments.

Also, the encounters are really badly repetitive. It's always a manufacturing plant, or a minor settlement, or an abandoned base, with negligible differences. After 3-4 encounters it's as much fun as rubbing sandpaper against your skin.

Finally, EVERY space station is the same. In a game where you can visit practically unlimited number of star systems and travel across the galaxy, EVERY space station is the same. Wow again. Would it be that difficult to make a proper procedural system that assembles stations from basic elements? Even 20 years ago we had games like Diablo 2 that could seamlessly generate entire maps.

Space ships don't seem to differ either in major ways, besides their annoying inventory layouts. There is just no comparison to proper space games like Elite: Dangerous (which I also don't like btw, because it has hardly anything else to offer). Ship handling and automatic landing is a joke. I'm sorry, but it is.

I tried to like the game, but it left me scratching my head. I think the devs really badly neglected the most fundamental game mechanics while adding a crapload of features. This game must have a very specific audience; people who love repetition, or just can't notice it.

My friends and I were looking for something to do, so we decided to buy No Man's Sky. 

The first mistake.

The entire first hour of gameplay consisted of feeble attempts to join the stars among the ether of space, only to die over and over and over to heat, suffocation, and terrible, terrible robots. 

Our first planet we started on was absolute hell to traverse, as we needed to find scarce materials in order to stay alive to complete any sort of objective, and right when we would find sodium to recharge our heat protection, our life support systems would die.

The game is tedious and boring after the first five minutes of playing in a state of wonder at the world before you.

I was under the impression that the game had undergone a drastic metamorphosis after the trainwreck release, but I was sorely disappointed. There is so little to do in the game without getting annoyed with just about every part of the game.

In a game inclusive of soaring through the cosmos, the ship feels like playing skee-ball but the lane you roll the ball against is made of ice and someone oiled the ice. The target is also always smaller than the ball, so you're guaranteed to never, ever land your shots on enemy pirates.

No part of me wants to return to No Man's Sky, and I would much rather break my own knees with a cast-iron skillet than play another minute of this awful, awful game.

If you don't already know what the game's about but are interested, think about it kinda like a nice blend between Destiny and Minecraft. You can spend the same amount of hours exploring and building bases as you can trying to find exotics and high tier or end game items/upgrades. If you could fly your ship in destiny it would feel kinda like this.

Everything you do can feel like progression, whatever you do, however you choose to do it, can take you on an adventure you never expected. At any point you can verge off the main quests and figure things out yourself.

The crossplay update is really what tied it all together, the game now feels even better than what they promised, the mechanics are streamlined, easily accessable, and fleshed out to work well with existing game mechanics.

This game might as well be a miracle. Its a technological achievement on its own and you had Sony rush this thing out like an uncooked steak on an early access platter. Very little faith was in the game right after release but update after update you could see their vision coming to life and now you'll find all sorts of people in this game. younger kids who mostly explore and have their first gamer moments. Gamers that reach their own ultimate conclusion via their own goals or the games goals. Base builders, loot goblins, completionists, even people who just want that relaxing escape in their day to day stress.

Content synergy. Just as you can create a badass mech or use your one-of-a-kind ship to take on the robot space police, you can trade, buy and scrap ships, harvest your own fortunes, warp system to system for thousands of lightyears, and at any time you can find and join friends and teleport to pretty much anywhere you've been before, do the same missions with them and create a unique and vast experience.

Its ready. You wont have to restart characters as often as when the main updates were flying in, you can safely commit to 100hrs of gameplay on the same character and not really worry about your progress or having to make new characters. This game is DEEP, and sometimes it can take a while to get exactly what you want.

My only negative is that this game will make time fly faster than if you were in a coma. Hey it was 10:30 when I last checked now its 2pm. and during that time you either can get a lot done or almost nothing with the same level of immersion and lack of awareness of time. Yet it doesnt feel like your grinding things out like a typical mmorpg or similar grind. you spread your wings quick but the universe is the limit, sometimes overwhelming, you can experience as much or as little of it as you want, and there will always be more.

While I have had fun, it often comes in spite of the game rather because of it. 

The UI makes every interaction with the game a chore. The UI is as if someone tried to take the worst parts of a PC and console game and mash them together. You must use a cursor (Destiny-style) even with a controller. But menus and options must be scrolled through one at a time as if you're using a controller, rather than a mouse. Item storage is broken into multiple tabs and you can't easily drag/drop/rearrange items. Inventory menu opens to a seemingly random inventory option (backpack/starship/multitool) The only constant is that its  *never* the one I want to access.

While game offers dozens and dozens of different items, technology and consumables, inventory space is at an extreme premium. And I'm told this is already after significant enhancements were made to the game, apparently it used to be far worse. The game does not offer a "chest" for additional storage, making bases seemingly pointless. Only 10 storage containers, which do not act like chests, but rather awkwardly accessed backpack upgrades (all "0" storage containers share the same 20 slots no matter which "0" storage container you access)

Exploration is fun, playing with friends is fun, getting new stuff is fun. But the above issues really drag down everything else.

After the shitstorm release of 2016 No Mans Sky lost all my trust as a video game. All I saw was an empty god forsaken puddle that was an inch shallow. Obviously the Hello Games was not prepared to release this to the public for many reasons. Fast forward to 2020 and it shines bright as a fine example of a developer taking care of their players. Hello Games isn't some multi-billionaire company that can dump a bunch of money into development but damn do they act like one. The game is not riddled with microtransaction trash...if there is micros I havn't found it yet. The game is saturated with great content that rewards players who explore. My character is a Gek Mechanic who resides in a scrapyard (that I built) on a barren planet within a yellow star solar system. I comb my planet, system and others to find broken down ships and stranded explorers to either take the ship and repair it myself or lend a hand to the deserted aliens. Whether its fixing up a ship for cash, repairing a multitool, scrapping near by crashed freighters or trading with my fellow Geks. I (as a character) am presented with opportunity and choices that fit my role as a scavenger. Many encounters, minor settlements, abandoned buildings, trade outposts, alien structures, sentinel bases, crashed ships, stranded aliens, exosuit pods, and many more await to be discovered. I cannot tell you how many times I was presented with a new encounter where my reaction was filled with curiosity. Each encounter comes with dialogue which was written by someone who deeply cares about immersive experiences and reading them helps me dive deeper in not only my character but the universe of No Mans Sky itself.

TLDR - Game sucked in 2016. Game is a Shining Diamond in the AAA Trash we have today in 2020. Look past the rough release and buy it. On sale or not Id buy this game at 60$.

4/5 - Explore / Discovery / Crafting / Building

The thing that this game does better than anything else is the sense of immersion. The rumble of the starship as you engage pulse drive, the roar of a firestorm as you scramble for shelter on a hostile planet, the sheer awe of countless vistas and beautiful places are like nothing I've ever seen before.

The universe of No Man's Sky is truly massive, with so much to do in each system that you could play most of the game without ever needing to stray too far beyond your original home star. To be fair, often times many of the worlds can feel repetitive, with similar looking animals or plants.

But ultimately, I think this game, like all games, depends on what you make of it, and with a game this vast, there's always plenty to do and see. 

Buy this game if you:
-Enjoy being immersed in a massively complex space fantasy universe
-Like building, upgrading, and using bases, ships, and weapons
-Like resource collection and refinement mechanics (mining minerals, farming, etc)
-Enjoy the idea of exploring uncharted worlds and cataloging the flora and fauna for all of science
-Want to live out a life as a mercenary or pirate, either as a lone renegade or part of a coordinated fleet
-Enjoy trading resources and materials to make a hefty profit
-Driving sweet vehicles like rovers and mech suits

Don't buy this game if you:
-don't really vibe with space games
-don't enjoy open-world or open-ended games
-don't like how many features that were originally promised still haven't made it into the game, or are present with bugs
-think $60 is too much for what's offered

PROS:
- Impressive turnaround for a game that originally went down in history as one of the most disappointing video game releases ever.
- Not too high of a learning curve to figure out how to actually play the game, thanks to a flowing tutorial
- Highly addicting game mechanics that almost makes you feel like you aren't grinding hours away at a time.
- Soundtrack kicks serious a** and its fun enough to listen to it by itself. 

CONS:
- The whole point of the game is to travel to hundreds of procedurally generated planets, yet in the first six hours I have just now made it to my third planet because of all the stuff you can do / need to do
- The resource/crafting system requires a lot of recipe memorization and it can take a lot of time just to get the final ingredient you need
- I haven't played multiplayer yet but so far trying to make it by myself is lonesome and gets dull after a while.

Overall, this game has REALLY turned itself around from the garbage fire everyone said it was from years ago. I have not had any crashes or loss of progress (yet) and I am running on a modest gaming laptop.

Tbh I've never really enjoyed no mans sky before I tried it in VR. Highly recommend this game if you have VR, and if you don't have VR and aren't completely burnt out of the survival-exploration genre of games this game has turned into a pretty good one. Reviews.130676:
Yes it had a rough start.  Yes there were a lot of things promised that weren't there, but they have worked hard to bring us much of what was lacking, and the game is much better for it!

If you are expecting this game to be a fast-paced  sci-fi thrill ride, you will be disappointed.  Yet if you play it for what it is, a game heavily focused on exploration, and don't mind a slower pace starting out, you might be like me and learn to really like it.  I find it great when I want something casual, and laid back.  Sure, it gets a bit annoying starting out with having to repair your equipment seemingly way too often.  Yet once you get on a planet with a decent environment, that isn't such an issue.  Then you get vehicles (look up how to get them as I could have gotten many days earlier if I had know it).  They help a lot.

Tips
1. Early on, don't worry about hanging onto everything.  You can't.  Find stuff that has a high value (tooltips tell you).  Trash the low value stuff, and load up your bags with high value stuff.  Then go sell it at a space station.
2. The stuff you need to fuel your ship (Tritium) can be found shooting up asteroids and the crystal formations stuck to them, just beyond your planets atmosphere!  Easy to farm. 
3. Scan for and get buried technology.  Use them to buy blueprints of crafted items (buildings, vehicles, etc.) 

Don't trust the haters.  Some people never forgive, and some people think their opinion should be they only one, attempting to peddle it as the truth.  If you are intrigued, then watch some peeps on Twitch.  Ask questions, and learn.  Find out for yourself if the game is good for you.  Good luck all!

I've followed this game since the VGX trailer way back in 2013. I was captivated by the concept from the get-go and followed every interview and trailer up to release. Bought it on GOG in August 2016 and was captivated by those first 10+ hours. But as I spent more time with it, I definitely began to feel underwhelmed. It felt like a demo of what the concept could be, a lonely exploration game with a strong focus on truly varied procedural environments. I remember thinking, though, that I could still see the passion behind it, and I wanted to see the developers stick with the game.

After 3 years, I can say that the game truly evolved into something worth your time. I don't think it quite captures the original vision I felt from the initial trailers, but that's okay. It's more "expressive tools in a extremely large and varied sandbox" than "discovery of completely unique environments". Their procedural generation is clearly ahead of most other games, but it's kind of fascinating how quickly people can still spot and recognize common elements.  

I find myself consistently coming back and playing this game across multiple platforms, seeing what they've expanded upon. To me, No Man's Sky truly captures the artistic spirit of games, combining innovative technology with expression, achieved by a team that closely knows one another. 

Thank you Hello Games, for being an example of what dedication, passion, and truly listening to the feedback of a community can achieve.

This game does not feel like a finished product. I want to play it, but it doesn't want me to play it. 6 hours in and I've had 2 save files which became infinite death loops upon loading, among other annoying buggy experiences.

I also think the game has a very flawed progression system. It feels like I'm forced to follow a very long tutorial, yet the tutorial does not feel very intuitive at all for first 30 minutes, where I literally started the game by dying because my planet was too hot.

I have to complain about the saving system. It's the weirdest one I've ever seen in a game. When you go to close the game, it tells you your last save was x minutes ago, are you sure you want to close? But it doesn't offer to save the game, and it wasn't clear to me that there was any way to save the game at all. After googling it, I found out that you have to craft a portable save point in the game to save. But the easiest way to save is actually to exit your ship, because the game will always auto save when you do that. So the game wants saving to cost you in game, it wants to put me through a long hand-holding tutorial, yet it I don't recall it ever teaching me how to save. Yet it also auto-saves fairly regularly? This game wants to have it both ways. It wants to let you save, but it doesn't. It wants to hold your hand, but it wants you to die right off the bat.

There's definitely enjoyment to be found in this game, but I would absolutely not pay $60 for the game in this state. I only paid $30 and I still might try to get a refund.

Wow. 12 hours in and I am completely hooked. I've been looking for a space themed game where you have control of everything and access to an open world... No Man's Sky delivers! I have tried playing so many space exploration type games that just didn't do it for me. Most space sim games are fighters and space battles with a lot of complicated controls where you have to spend at least a week just to get the basics.

This game uses damn near every key on the keyboard also. However, I got pretty comfortable with the controls within the first hour. If I had to complain about something, it would be that sometimes it is hard to figure out where you're going or how to craft something, where you're supposed to put it after you craft it (to make use of it), etc... But fumbling around a bit will usually get you moving forward (as well as a quick google search).

No Man's Sky reminds me a lot of Subnautica (another game I truly love playing). You have to pay attention to your surroundings... is the air toxic? Are the temperatures bearable? I love it. Scan a planet before you land and be prepared for how you will need to deal with those things. Crafting items to upgrade parts of your gear (as well as your starship and ground vehicles) is fun. I do wish sometimes it didn't take so many steps to get to that upgrade sometimes, especially when it is something you need in order to proceed in your current quest. But it is still a LOT of fun. And when you're stuck, usually you'll see a popup in the right side of your screen that hints at what you're supposed to be doing or where you're going.

Graphics are blessedly amazing and I like the sound effects. I like how the ground shakes when other starships fly over at low altitude. I started off playing in "Creation" mode (I am so glad the dev put this mode in here). I wanted to start there to get comfortable with the controls and how everything works before throwing myself out there to try and survive. Fly to new space stations, see other aliens with their ships. Like their ship better? Offer to buy it from them!

Reviews.130877:
A lot of people still remember this game for its disappointing launch but a lot has changed since then with Hello Games releasing many large (free) content updates over the years and are even continuing to do so to this day almost four years after release.

No Man's Sky's procedurally generated universe creates seemingly endless replayability. There's a number of story missions and lore to discover, plenty of things to unlock and rare equipment and ships to obtain. Exocraft also offer an alternative to on foot (or jetpack) travel to make getting around and collecting resources less tedious. Base building is great, allowing for some really elaborate bases and teleporters allow you to easily travel between your bases and to space stations in different galaxies. There's also missions available on the Space Anomaly which can be completed with other players or solo, the weekend missions give you extra rewards so there's an added incentive to return to No Man's Sky.

If you're playing with friends or into base building you'll get even more out of this game, I've been playing solo and found base building a lot more fun than I had anticipated. I definitely recommend this game to those interested, the 50% off sale lately is worth it for sure.

No Man's Sky has come a long way since its release. It's a game that has been hated, improved, given a second, and well deserved chance, and will keep improving and updating (hopefully for a long time). The devs keep working on NMS, adding new things for free, unlike many other developers. 

I strongly recommend NMS to gamers, who love exploring, grinding, collecting, and overall the chill sandbox experience. Because man does this game delivers when it comes to that. 
You discover new planets, new elements, creatures, minerals etc... you even learn languages. You can cook, build, collect space ships, grow your space fleet, and so many many things. There is really a lot to do in this game, and it will keep you entertained for a long period of time. 

I do have to mention a few negative things though. 
  - There are still some bugs, that have existed for a while, but haven't been fixed - for example the one where you sink trough the ground. 
  - Planets get quite repetitive. The types of planets all have the same looking plants and minerals, and creatures but with different names.
  - Missions could have a bit more variety as well.

All in all, I have quite enjoyed this game, and I advise you to give it a go.

Reviews.130969:
[h1]Worst gameplay I've ever experienced[/h1]

Although I knew about the horrible start of this game I've also seen plenty of comments and Youtube videos which explained how this game managed to "[i]re-invent itself[/i]"; what was first a horrible game had evolved into a good game, or so they said. The Steam summer sale is upon us (yay!) and with a 50% discount I figured I'd take a gamble. Now I wish I hadn't because even at 50% off this game is definitely [u]not[/u] worth it in my opinion.

So I start a new, casual, game. I end up on a planet and it tells me to scan the area but uh oh: my scanner is broken. Now I need to collect 'something' to repair it. But how I am supposed to do that doesn't get explained. What all the numbers and such on my HUD are telling me doesn't get explained, [u]nothing[/u] gets explained. Assuming I must be on some kind of tutorial world I start searching my surroundings; having seen Youtube videos I know that you need to use your laser to gather resources so.. that's what I'm doing. Of course the stuff I'm after is no where in sight.

After 5 or so minutes I finally managed to find what I'm looking for. While the game hinted at "small yellow flowers" I'm actually shooting some kind of mineral and....   then I die, for reasons I completely fail to understand. Sorta... the game (or your suit?) does constantly warn about radiation damage and such, but it doesn't explain how I am supposed to avoid all that.

[h1]No tutorial, no explanations, you're thrown in the deep; "thanks for buying?"[/h1]

Yes, I am well aware that if you hit escape then you can open a tutorial section. The game never told me but I found out on my own. Was it really too difficult to add some kind of in-game pointer to this? It gets worse.. the tutorial pages I [i]did[/i] read [u]made [b]no[/b] sense what so ever[/u]. And being a vivid guide writer myself I know [i]exactly[/i] why that is so: because it was written by someone who knows the game inside out but doesn't even bother [b]trying[/b] to keep new players in mind. You know... the kind of player who [u]doesn't[/u] understand all the gameplay mechanics yet?

Survival basics: "[i]Hazard protection is vital, carry Sodium or Ion Batteries[/i]". Just too bad that the game doesn't bother to carefully explain where I can get those and to add insult to injury the game also doesn't bother to drop me on some kind of starter planet where there's no immediate need for this.

[h1]Horrible, [u]horrible[/u] gameplay[/h1]

Sure... a survival game doesn't have to be easy but why do I constantly need to sustain myself in an exploration game? As far as I know I am wearing a radiation suit and those are normally designed to keep radiation out. If I'm not wearing one then why am I even out here in space in the first place? It makes no sense other than: gameplot. The game needs this in order to make the gameplay more difficult than it should be.

But making things difficult just for the sake of it does [u]not[/u] account for good gameplay, quite the opposite even!

[h1]Inconsistent and thus highly annoying controls...[/h1]

"Click here", but in reality the game means: "Click and hold the mouse button here". I can somewhat understand why they did this, it definitely prevents clicking options by accident. If only....   if only they continued using this mechanic in screens where there's a real risk of clicking stuff by mistake; for example when you need to decide which parts of a device you're going to repair. Yah, but then it's suddenly "click, you're done!". [u]Why?!![/u].  Menu options which are seriously hard to overlook need to be confirmed by holding your mouse button and small options which can easily be clicked by accident... can simply be clicked.

[h1]It wasn't a fluke experience....[/h1]

It was worse: totally by design.

Just in case you're wondering "[i]Shell, you were simply unlucky and if you had tried again you'd notice that things aren't all that bad![/i]" then please think again....  I restarted my game [u]4 times[/u][/i] and [b]every time[/b] I ended up on some kind of radiated planet where I had to avoid radiation while the game never bothered to tell me how I was supposed to do that. Sure... it told me to seek shelter in caves, but when I tried to enter one it made my radiation meter go up.

I did eventually find a damaged ship, with a distress beacon. So when I learned that the "only thing" I had to do was to gather more resources to fix the ship I closed the game and started writing off my anxiety, you see the results before you.

Sure... let's gather resources to repair my ship while the game never did so much as to teach me some basic survival!

[h1]This game is [u]severely[/u] overpriced if you ask me....[/h1]

Even with a 50% discount... I can't believe this (old) game normally sells at triple A pricing, it totally baffles me considering the poor interface, the lack of any kind of tutorial what so ever, the risk of dying within the first 5 minutes of this game without even understanding why, a constant need to gather resources but you don't get any clue what you're collecting and what for, confusing inventory controls....

I could go on for a while but I got better things to do, I'm not wasting any more time than I need on this.

I highly recommend you stay as far away from this game as you can. There is no real gameplay here, let alone balanced gameplay (LOL!). For me it's just one huge frustrating mess of a game. The only thing I am thankful for is that I know Steam will allow me to request a refund, the first refund I've done in 2020.

[h1]In conclusion....[/h1]

What a horrible disappointment this was :(

I didn't expect a brilliant game, but I also didn't expect things to be this bad; overpriced, non-existent gameplay, highly unfriendly towards new players....   this game is a total mess.
Reviews.130970:
Been playing No Man's Sky since day one. Early versions of the game weren't bad, but were very bland/empty. The team has really brought the game a long ways from those early days. It really has grown into an impressive and extensive game, although I would argue it still falls a little short of what it could be. 

The biggest thing for me was the added VR support. It really brought this game front and center for me, and to that end, it's one of the best VR games I've got to play, in my opinion. The overall pacing of the game lends itself really well to VR, and overall I'd say it's a pretty enjoyable experience. 

In it's current form, there's more game there then I've even got a chance to fully explore. With that being said though, I don't always feel like there's much in the universe driving you forward to anything. You can blaze your own path, and find your own goals, but sometimes it kind of boils down to finding things to do, out of a need to do something for the sake of doing something. It can be meandering.  

Lastly, I think the overall combat/conflict in the game is weak, and is one of the aspects of the game I really dislike. In space, I don't like engaging in space battles in VR, because I don't really find the controls to be all that precise when compared to like, if you were using a gamepad. Because you aren't holding onto a physical flight stick, your hand tends to float around a little, and for me it just doesn't work out all that well. It makes me hate actually being in space, because of the number of random enemy ships that'll spawn and attack you. It's especially frustrating when I'm trying to repair ships from my fleet, because I can't repair them while an enemy ship is about. It gets tedious. I don't want to engage the enemy because of the time sink and poor flight controls, so I end up doing this dance where I exit the area completely, dink around, then come back, and hope the area is reset enough to do a repair before the next enemy ship decides to spawn. 

On the ground, you can get into fights with the local robots, but I just don't see the point of any of it. The main issue is they're just an omni-present thing. You might have to fend them off when accessing certain resources (which is fine/good), but other than that there's no real depth to them. 

Which leads into my biggest issue with the combat in this game. There's just no real point to it, other than for the sake of conflict. I don't feel like I gain anything by engaging in conflict. It's just too paper-thin of a mechanic. There's all these resources for adding versatility and variety to your weapons, via the gun or ship, but what does it really get you in the end when the combat isn't fun or rewarding? 

I think No Man's Sky, as it is today, would benefit from an enemy setup kind of like Terraria. Right now, it's more of a defensive game, as it relates to combat, but if you had swarms you had to worry about, or bosses you could seek down and fight. Something that draws you into combat, that makes you seek it out, and really embrace that side of the game. 

For example, if I needed a rare resource I could only get from the pirate colonies. It'd be awesome. You could be diplomatic about it, perhaps, or you could plan an all out raid. Build up your weapons, your shields for your ship. Go to the space stations and get info to track one of the colonies down, then raid it. 

Still an overall great game though, and I'd especially recommend it if you're looking for a full gaming experience in VR.

This game took a lot of flack in the beginning, and I skipped it. Not entirely voluntarily, either - I run Linux only on my computers (and intend to stay that way), and I didn't buy a PS4. It wasn't until a recent sale that I decided to give it a shot and see how it runs in Proton. And I was pleasantly surprised, no doubt thanks to their continued work on the game, having converted the renderer to Vulkan, which makes Proton's job that much easier.

This is one of those games that I thought I'd enjoy, but wasn't aware of just how much I would.
It isn't similar in gameplay, setting, narrative, etc. to games like Oblivion, Skyrim, or the modern Fallout games, and yet, I lump it in a similar category as them in the sense that I find them low-stress, enjoyable, easy to lose myself and my time in them. The hours melt away as I explore vast worlds.

The combat is just okay, but I am having fun exploring, finding new planets, scanning everything (reminds me a little of Metroid Prime in that regard), crafting, doing missions, finding new ships, etc. Being able to hop into my ship and fly from one planet to the next without any load screens is amazing, and the load screens that do exist are thematically appropriate, showing your ship warping or crazy colours as you teleport from outpost to base to outpost. It feels very seamless, and I feel it's quite a feat.

That said, I don't think it's a game for everyone. But if you think you'd like it based on what you've seen in videos, you probably will.

TLDR: 
A procedural science fiction exploration and survival game. Planets have their own ecosystems and dangers. Different space- and exocraft to explore in under water, on land and in space. The game features base-building and a crafting system relying heavily on resource gathering. There is a story although a bit thin and quests/missions to complete. Also possible to own your own fleet and send them on missions. 

As it is now, i would rate it 8/10.

So, No Man's Sky... The game i followed since it was first announced. 
A lot was promised. Though on release, it was clear that a lot of those promises were simply not lived up to. 
This left a bitter taste in my mouth and, dissapointed as i was, i decided to skip this game entirely. 

Here we are now, 4 years later and wow... how the developers have turned things around. I can honestly now really recommend this game to anyone that likes exploration in space games.

Please bear in mind that i did not play this game for thousands of hours. Im about 50 hours in so that could be considered as not much. Still, i feel i have played enough hours to give my honest opinion about it.

Gameplay:
The 4 main pillars that build up No Man's Sky Gameplay consist of Exploration, Combat, Trade and Survival. At the start of the game you can choose from 4 modes: Normal, Survival, Permadeath and Creative. 

- Normal is the original mode of play when the game was released and is labeled as a 'chill exploration experience'. Regular 
  difficulty, standard technology and building costs.
- Survival provides a more challenging survival experience with limited recources, increased hazards and stronger, more 
  aggressive enemies.
- Permadeath is just survival mode with the added consequence of dead is dead. Its just that, die and you have to start over.
- Creative allows you to play with unlimited health and resources and zero building costs.

The gameplay loop consists of gathering materials and crafting stuff which you can then use to do stuff. Be it building a base or travelling the galaxy. You will find yourself doing a lot of resource gathering which does make the game feel grindy at times. 
The crafting consists of refining and combining materials. You can build your bases on land and underwater and even up in the sky. The galaxy is completely procedurally generated where planets have their own ecosystems and dangers.

The game offers different spaceships consisting of shuttles, fighters, explorers, haulers, exotics and even living ships. To continue your exploration on the surface or underwater you can build different sizes of exocraft, a submersible vehicle and even a walking mech.

All your ships and vehicles including your space suit are upgradeable in inventory and technology slots and allow you to install different tech to improve them.

It is also possible to own your own fleet and send them on different themed missions throughout the galaxy.

There are a few main questlines you can follow which are interesting although a bit shallow.

Multiplayer:
There is cross-platform multiplayer ingame now. You can join up with multiple players from steam, xbox and playstation and share a galaxy. It is possible to build bases together. There also is a multiplayer hub in the game which you can summon in space after completing a few quests where you can meet other players and go on missions with them.

Graphics:
The comic style graphics are inspired by old sci-fi art. Lots of vibrant, bright colors bring the different planets and locations you can visit to life. Though not a particular impressing game graphically, it's style does give it a rather timeless aesthetic.

Sound:
The new-age electronic music really fits the slow pace of the game with some more epic battle music when in combat. Paired with the "simple" sound effects it really complements the visual style of the game.

Ive played this game since it was released. at first i was very disappointed with the false promises that were made and the clearly staged trailer footage but at the same time I still enjoyed the game a great deal just for the exploring aspect of it. After reaching the center of the galaxy and getting the best ship and multitool available the game lost its appeal.
fast forward to the current version of the game. many big updates ALL FREE and now the game feels like what I had hoped it to be and more.

At first I thought that the ability to build bases was pointless cause it is an exploration game, but now that I have played it further and understand what is going on I see that between being able to teleport your base to another location, and having teleport portals to allow you to move materials over distance it makes it feel less redundant. I am enjoying the ability to terraform and build and farm and raise critters and multiplayer and everything that comes along with it.

I think right now my biggest disappointments is that the universe is still infinite and randomly stumbling upon other players is still very unlikely. I think something the devs could do to make it feel less lonely is to copy players bases and have them randomly appear in other locations for other players to find perhaps with little messages to indicate where they came from.

another thing I would like to see added is a better galaxy map. currently you need to be in space to access it and navigating is seemingly impossible.

the npc's are still very 1 dimensional as well, in general i dont even care what they have to say, I just skip through the conversation until they offer to teach me something or give me something.

Anywho, games not too hard to get in to as a new player and the tutorial is definitely helpful as are the missions that guide you through all the new things you can do.

So many people say the game is finally "fixed", but from my experience it really isn't. My main problem is still the lack of a story or goal that it has missed since launch.
"You set your own goals" is the type of stuff that sandbox games tell you, but it really only works when you're actually given the tools to actually make an impact.
Sure, the game lets you build bases, upgrade ships and buy freighters now, but they all just seem like meaningless tasks to keep you occupied from the lack of a real goal to strive towards.

The game wants to be multiple things at the same time, but in trying, falls behind in every way.
You can play as a pirate, but once you've destroyed one freighter, you've destroyed them all.
You can play as a trader, but every space station is the same and the prices don't even fluctuate that much.
You can play it for the story-mode, which has no structure or fulfilling ending.
You can play as a base-builder, but all the things you want are locked behind a research and resource grind-wall.
Or you can play as a combination of all (which seems to be the intended way) and still feel lackluster in all the same ways.

It's not about the destination, but the journey, which is all well and good when your destination is more complex than an icon on your HUD.
When your goal is as simple as "Go here" or "Mine this", the journey really reflects that too.
For instance, I was on my way to find a cactus I needed for a researcher at my base, but along the way I found a destroyed freighter in space.
I immediately stopped to inspect it, but after searching everywhere around it for even the slightest interaction, I gave up and just went on to get the cactus, and then went home.
Some subtle clue as to why it was destroyed would have at least given me something to chew on, something to do as a distraction, to set up further interactions.
Maybe it was in a fight with a pirate that I can then hunt down to enact revenge? Maybe it was attacked by some unknown being or carrying some special cargo?
But as it was, the little stop during my pulse-drive was just as boring and meaningless as my destination was.

The universe may be procedural, but none of the stuff you do in it is.
You keep doing the same things, over and over, expecting that some of your questions are eventually answered and lead to some exciting discovery, but they never do.
What is that green slime i keep seeing? Why has this freighter crashed and what is this portal doing here?
The only glimpses of lore you get are from the 2-line dialogue-boxes you get when interacting with other entities or terminals.
Most of these are either descriptions of the people: "The Vykeen seems unhappy at my presence" or some simple dialogue: "Go away traveller", which doesn't exactly answer anything.
I understand that not everything can be explained fully, like the atlas core which is supposed to be a mysterious entity etc.
But giving just the tiniest piece of lore might go a long way to keep players interested or, at the very least, giving me something to distract myself with on my way to the next grind.
It doesn't need to be directly told by some other entity, it could just be a recording or a note, giving you insight into what the people at this crashed ship/abandonded facility were doing etc.
As it is right now, the game has not been fixed. My problem was never that it didn't have multiplayer or base-building or a number of other features that were never promised.
My problem is the lack of any connection between the gameplay and the story, of answers to questions you have about the planet you're exploring, of anything that really makes the universe feel alive and lived in.

I started this game thinking that it's basically a good story in a massive randomly generated universe. It's true that there are loads of planets each slightly different from each other. It's also true that there is a story. But, once you've been on a few planets you'll notice that they are basically all the same. Slightly different colours and texture of the surface, different number of animal species and different number of plant species. I did the Atlas path part of the story, which basically amounts to getting you to travel from one space station to another with each being basically the same (with small variations). The story is a text box that comes up when you reach the next checkpoint. I kept hoping that there'd be more and it'd get more interesting, but it just didn't so eventually I just gave up. 

In terms of building the base, the base has quite a lot of different components you can add. I personally didn't find it to be lots of fun though because of how much grinding it takes to actually gather enough materials to build the base. 

People you encounter are all the same, they have a random helmet and clothes and are of a random species and say a piece of random text. If you want to understand what they are saying, you can grind to decode their language one word at a time. 

Caveat: After the boredom I experienced, I didn't continue with the Artemis Path. Maybe that's more fun, but after hours of thinking this whilst being bored I just don't believe it anymore. 

My overall feedback is that the game is cool but it just isn't that much fun to play.

So I tried this after the first big revamp and found it functional but... well... boring. 

I tried to give it another go, and figured "Hey, let's try Hardcore to make it a bit more exciting".

Here's the thing: As far as I can tell, you always start on a radiated/thermal extreme planet so you have to prioritize finding Sodium plants for... quite a bit, tbh. In a normal game, annoying; in a hardcore game, I died three times due to unable to find Sodium plants to keep my hazard protection up enough to get to my broken ship (which you can huddle in to get back your Hazard protection for free). This was mainly just annoying (since it's supposed to be the tutorial area, but resources were insufficient to survive).

The real killer for me was getting off the first planet:
You get a signal to go to another planet in the system, where you get some tutorial for base building mechanics. I got sent to a planet where the Hazard was AGGRESSIVE SENTINELS. Immediately when I landed, a sentinel pops up, scans me, and starts attacking. It turns out they don't de-aggro if you hide in your ship; they just wait.

So I used my mining laser to slowly kill it. 10 seconds later, more arrive (think getting another star in GTA style). Great. Now I'm stuck in my ship, and surrounded by a small army who now has armor plating. I can't take off, since apparently my ship's full fuel tank = 1 liftoff for some reason (I had a half tank and it told me insufficient fuel).

I jump out of my ship and barrel for the hills, barely surviving. Eventually I escape the Sentinels (losing LOS starts a timer for them to give up); the small army calls off, but while I'm running, three more sentinels pop up from the brush and start to scan/follow me. This continues until I am so far away from my ship and my objective that it takes a good hour of just trying to make my way back (they chase you hecka far, and have BS LOS rules).

After carefully, anxiously, doing my mining and whatnot tutorials, I now have a small hut with a research unit, a refiner outside and a base cpu outside. But... my place is literally always swarmed with Sentinels (they don't seem to come into your base at least) and I need to access things.

So, I run outside, pick up the refiner and put it in the hut.

I run back outside and quickly interact with the CPU to try to move it so I don't killed doing the tutorial objectives. It turns out you can only "Delete Base", which gives no warning dialogues of what that actually means.

It means it deletes every thing you have placed within the... "base area" which seems ill-defined.

My entire base immediately disappears. Everything. Just me and about 4 Sentinels.

Total bullshit, I've since uninstalled.

Oh, and it tells you how to place a custom marker, but not remove it. So that custom marker will be on your HUD forever, even on other planets, because Fuck You apparently.

From a 2016 veteran, here is my opinion on this game (TL;DR at the bottom):

In 2016, I received this game as a birthday gift. I remember joining the hype and seeing how much was promised in the beginning and how excited I was to get this game. My brother bought it for me on the PS4 before I had a gaming computer. Despite the lack of content (that was lied about), I really REALLY enjoyed the game. I was one of the few who seriously played for hours upon hours. Something about exploring a vast universe and being a pathfinder in endless space is really really awesome to me, no matter how simple the gameplay is.

However, that obsession eventually died out. I saw the game as sort of a canvas to be worked on- which was naive to some extent. This was before I saw the tragedy of the gaming industry and the disgusting abandonware stuff that exists.

In the end, I can see my gamble on the perspective and the thought of 'it will grow into something even more amazing' paid off. This game has grown into something seriously special. Hello Games could've taken the money and run, they could've just given the bird and that would've been that. However, they instead fixed their game and made it something fantastic.

This game truthfully fulfills all of the niches I could've wanted in a game. Trading, farming, path-finding new worlds to colonize, being a fleet captain, exploring with friends, jumping around in a giant mech, and more recently the ability to explore the universe with people across other platforms- linking the playerbase at large.

If none of that convinces you, please just go watch some videos on it and see some of the amazing content for yourself. This game offers hundreds of hours easily if you wish to max out everything and have many adventures- Sorvon Inc. invites you, and if you choose to join- we welcome you!

TL;DR: Once a failure, and was one of the biggest disappointments in gaming history (not in my opinion however), turned into one of the most unique experiences that is absolutely amazing.

So, here's the thing.

I came out of 2016, hearing of the glorious flop of a game, known to all as No Man's Sky. A game where a company lied and stole from the community, hurting the hype filled fan base and launching them into the ground at breakneck speed, only to take the money and disappear.
Back then, it was fun to laugh at and hate on this game, this was the game to hate.

It has been a long time since then, and Hello Games took all that money they made off of this game, and instead of running away with it, taking it and working on a new title, maybe rebranding themselves or letting someone else buy them out. They got to work, they made this game good.

Fast forward to now, Bethesda, A company I had trusted and loved for providing me with two of the greatest franchises ever made, has yet another Fallout 76 patch that sends its players into an uproar. That is the new game to hate. And instead of taking the money and getting back to work, they took it and ran with it, churning out more garbage and more depressing patches. I have almost lost all hope, I pray for the elder scrolls game which may never come...

But this company, an indie studio that was hated, hell, threatened with bomb threats, murder threats, and suffered the greatest beating of any dev to date... They turned around to the very community that shit all over them, and gave them a present.

That takes balls, Thank you Hello Games, for showing us that a company can care for its community. You have shown yourselves to be the good guys, and I respect you deeply.

For those of you who want to hear their story, The Internet Historian did a video on it. I suggest you check it out.

I first purchased this game after the NEXT update, which I am led to believe made the game Not Terrible, in that the earlier versions of the game were rather lackluster compared to what the original pitches had promised. But now, especially after the Beyond update in late 2019, this game is well worth playing.

This game is for you if you like:
- Exploring space!
- Decent but not groundbreaking sci-fi story
- Mysteries about the game's lore (I highly recommend *not* looking it up before you play, discovering it on your own is much more rewarding)
- Making bank as a commodities trader (or oddities trader!) as you warp between star systems

This game is not for you if you want:
- Realistic space physics. It always kinda bugs me that there's passive deceleration while in space in this game. Also orbital mechanics just flat out don't exist in this game.
- Challenging combat. There is some, but it's not *difficult*, at least not that I've encountered. Granted, I do tend to avoid combat, so perhaps there is challenging stuff sometimes. Maybe it's harder on the permadeath mode, too, I don't know. But most of the danger is in the form of environmental hazards, rather than aggressive enemies.
- Highly varied worlds. Although there's a massive amount of difference from world to world, each world seems to be the traditional sci-fi single-biome world. You get your desert worlds, your snow-covered worlds, your ocean worlds, your [REDACTED] worlds, and so on.

All in all, I think it's a worthwhile game to play. It might not be the best game ever made, but it's a good game. Maybe even a great game.

Note that I cannot comment on the multiplayer, as I do not like playing multiplayer in pretty much any game, so I have that turned off for this game.

[h1]Like a phoenix it has come back from the ashes of its initial release and has become something greater than it ever once was.[/h1]



For sure it's a staggering redemption story for this game, not to mention the tellings of what actually went down from its initial release.

From being forced to meet deadlines to needing to abandon, rush through, and even having a lot of what was said taken completely out of context-


... ... ... this game was set up to fail and burn on release... They were being propped up with no real hope of being able to meet expectations.

... but despite the initial release the game has received countless updates since, not just [b]QoL[/b] changes either.

As of this review it has received [b]nine[/b] content updates.


I joined in once the [b]Mech Update[/b] happened, which admittedly was a very light update compared to the others that have come before.

But regardless I feel this shows that the devs have a vision they want to see through to the end and do not want to just abandon this game and "run with the money" as some others tend to do.


My only two gripes that I've, personally, have had a problem with has been as-such:

-Practically all of the NPCs one adds to their base are rendered redundant in many ways, or really it's more to do with there's [b]many[/b] ways to get the same [b]research[/b] done. Almost too many.

-Graphically the game tends to have major pop-in occur from time to time, regardless of the settings. Though I will test things out once more now that I have a stronger card to work with. [i](2080Ti)[/i]


Regardless of this It's been a joy to play this game, building intricate bases, uploading them so the community can find and interact with them, seeing other's grand builds.

... and just in-general participating in the [b]Weekly Events[/b] that come around and seeing what else the Community has ended up creating.


[b][u]My closing thoughts are that:[/u][/b]

[i]-I hope in a future update we get a full [b]Variety Update[/b] that enhances and even re-defines some exploration mechanics.[/i]

[i]-I would like to see some of the more janky and unstable elements of the game be ironed out, Creature Movement, pathfinding, as well as terrain generation and the some-what rare crashes that still happen to this day.[/i]

[i]-While I do recommend this game I still feel that the $60 price point is a tad high for the unstable experience I've had. But I may just be very unlucky in this respect. But if the crash issues are to be ignored, yea I do feel that this game is now and will for sure be worth the $60 price point. Especially after the next coming updates for 2020![/i]

... ... ... just don't expect a lot of meaningful combat, though there's always the possibility that this can be touched on as well in the future.

[b]Hello Games[/b] has certainly earned my respect and I look forward to what they have planned next, not just with this game but with other projects they will involve themselves in.



[i]"Somewhere, something incredible is waiting to be known."[/i] -Carl Sagan

Also the game uses much less of my GPU and CPU proccesing power than I would have expected.

Overall this is an amazing game, with a pretty even structure, and an amazing concept.

I played this game with two of my friends. We initially had no real idea of what No Man's Sky was. I thought it's gonna be some kind of Minecraft in space: collecting, crafting, fighting a bit here and there, exploring the universe. Just like in those nice little trailers (where they use the same music over and over). But nope, this game is pure hell!

From the very first moment of the game everything is trying to kill you. It's incredibly stressful! The environment is always toxic, and each and every step you take costs oxygen and depletes your hazmat gear. That means you have to constantly search your environment for oxygen and protection, just so you can stay alive a few minutes longer. Besides staying alive, everything else costs resources too, even using your mining laser! There is nothing you can do without resources. If only your inventory were bigger! In addition, there are some kind of enemy drones. Sometimes they ignore you, most of the time they attack you, and if you are really unlucky they gather in numbers and make it impossible for you to get out of your ship/shelter without being killed. Me and my friends tried to teleport resources between each other, it sometimes worked, sometimes it didn't - for no apparent reason. 

The tutorial was lame, uninformative, and seemingly oblivious to that looming pressure of imminent death from the very first second I stepped on the surface of my randomly generated planet. And as if a dangerous surface, lack of oxygen and killer drones aren't enough, as soon as we took off from that hellish planet, fighter swarms were spawning everywhere and constantly attacked our hard to maneuver ships. 

This game isn't fun. It lacks a proper introduction, a calm starting area, and a humane level of difficulty. It's like starting a game you aren't familiar with on nightmare difficulty... and then being spawned in the lava pit.

Genuinely surprised how many positive reviews this has received.  I had assumed that the recent positivity meant they'd gotten past their poor launch.  Unfortunately all I've encountered are game breaking bugs, dull grind, and an interface that makes me want to cut my hands off.

The design of this game is just painful for the end user experience.  It feels like something that's tried to pad out content by intentionally making it take longer than it should for you to do anything.  The promotional videos suggest a fluidity to your gameplay that you just don't feel when playing it.  They're clearly heavily curated.  Don't get me wrong, there are parts of it that are beautiful, but I feel like this lot would've been better off creating an animated film with their resources than a game.

The user interface is a chore to use.  I'm surprised this made it to consoles given the layout - it's somehow managed to both be over simplified in terms of button use (a staple of cross platform games unfortunately) while also having too many distinct pages to jump around to so you have to keep flipping places to do organisation. TL;DR: Ive bought this game 2 times now and only regretted it the first time. Scratch that, it redeemed it self with the Beyond update, everything else after that just made me wanna buy it on PC.

Alright. There are many shady practices in the video game industry. In a world ravished by micro-transactions and big name companies, its nice to be reminded that there are still video game developers that truly care about the game more than their own personal gain. Was this one of the most absolute let downs of video game history? YES! But it was also one of the most hyped. The feeling of let down at launch is only partly to blame on the develops. SEAN MURRAY WHO!?!?!?! This dude, who mistakenly tripped into the triple A limelight one year at E3, was only doing what we as gamers do and he DREAMED. Out loud, infront of cameras, and ready to tell the world "hey guys, i got an idea." WE ATE THAT SHIT UP LIKE KAWASAKI!!!!!! So yea, we were ready to play a space game that wouldnt be so damn complex and polarizing (*cough* elite dangerous, star citizen, and X4 *cough*). Problem was, we were letting our imaginations run wild, while juicing this Sean Murray character up with all of our hypeness. He didnt know any better. He didnt understand that not only do you have to be exact when your talking about a game before its release, you cant tell the kids about how dope that present under the tree is before its the day to open it. SO come release day, and it was just an empty space game with nothing to do. Now? 4 years later? Numerous free expansions (yes expansions, although they are really just updates, the ammount changed could easily be counted as an expansion in todays market) legit multiplayer, and now true cross platform? PSH GET OUTTA HEEYA!!!! 

Now if your just coming back since launch, or playing for the first time, you really are going to be confused. THIS UNIVERSE MAY LOOK EMPTY AND DEAD AT TIMES, BUT THERE IS A BUTT LOAD OF THINGS GOING ON. Like building bases? The base building mechanic does take a little bit to get used to, but it isnt hard in the slightest. Base building not your thing? Start heading toward the center of the universe. Whats the point of that you ask? Well....let me just copy and paste the scope of this universe from the NMS wiki : "The universe of No Man's Sky comprises 255 unique galaxies, which in turn are comprised of around 3 to 4 billion regions, each of which contain more than 122 and up to hundreds of star systems. All star systems feature from 1-6 planets and moons, and usually a single space station. Players start in galaxy 1, Euclid, and travel through galaxies in order by reaching the Galaxy Centre or jump several by finishing the New Beginnings primary mission. After the player leaves galaxy 255 (Iousongola), they return to the first galaxy again." In other words, they had to add cross play to  populate one instance of this game in some way lol. 

 I suggest watching some videos on youtube of how to have a good start and different mechanics in the game. HawkesGaming and JasonPlays are 2 of my favorite NMS youtubers. This is no where near as complicated as Star Citizen or Elite Dangerous, and for sure gives you a much more simple time with economy and flight. Thats not to say this is a simple game or "easy." Its complex in its own ways. This is a game you can hand to a kid on creative and let them explore, and if that kid can get basic survival in minecraft down, they are completely capable of playing it on survival. Permadeath isnt so hard really, but it isnt a walk in the park. 

All in all, I absolutly love this game and since buying a new pc recently, ive fallen in love with this game more and more with ultra graphics. This game is perfect for any space cadet (you know who you are ;)) or survival game lovers alike.  BUY THIS ISH BOI!
